subcategories.title: Solar Cookers: Box, Panel, and Parabolic
subcategories.description: Three distinct designs for solar cookers — insulated box, uninsulated panel, and parabolic reflector — using common materials to cook food using the sun's energy.
subcategories.context: This module outlines three practical approaches to solar cooking. Each design serves a unique context — the box cooker for slow baking and minimal heat loss; the panel cooker for portability and simplicity; and the parabolic cooker for fast, high-heat applications. Best used in sunny, low-wind environments.

variants.optimalUse: Slow cooking, baking, grains, stews; suitable for long exposure (1.5–4 hrs) under strong sun; low burn risk.
materials: - Two cardboard boxes (one smaller, one larger)
- Insulation (crumpled newspaper, straw, wool, or recycled fabric)
- Aluminum foil or reflective mylar (for inside walls and flaps)
- Black, heat-safe paint (non-toxic, for pot exterior)
- Glass pane or clear oven bag (used to trap heat inside)
- Dark lidded cooking pot (thin black metal works best)
processSteps: 1. Nest smaller box inside larger, insulating all gaps between with newspaper or straw.
2. Line the inside of the inner box with foil (shiny side up), glued flat.
3. Paint the pot black and allow to dry fully.
4. Create an angled reflector lid using a flap cut into the outer box top, lined with foil.
5. Tape or hinge the reflector flap to adjust for best sun angle.
6. Cover top opening with clear oven bag or glass to retain heat.
7. Place food in the black pot, seal the cooker, and orient toward the sun.
8. Cook time varies from 1.5–4 hours depending on sun strength and dish type.

videos.title: Building a DIY Solar Box Cooker
videos.description: Step-by-step guide to constructing an insulated solar box cooker.

variants.optimalUse: Portable and lightweight; great for light cooking (e.g., reheating, tea, grains); ideal for community demos, emergency kits.
materials: - Clear oven bag or upside-down glass bowl
- Thin black pot or jar with tight-fitting lid
- Binder clips, tape, string, or glue
processSteps: 1. Cut reflective panels in 3–5 segments and hinge them at angles to form a reflector cone or C-shape.
2. Cover each panel with foil or reflective tape.
3. Place cooking pot inside a clear oven bag or under an inverted glass bowl.
4. Orient toward the sun, repositioning every 30–45 minutes for best results.
5. Monitor food through clear cover to prevent overheating or drying out.

videos.title: Making a Simple Solar Panel Cooker
videos.description: Demonstrates the construction of a basic, portable solar panel cooker.

variants.optimalUse: High heat applications (boiling water, frying, pressure cooking); great for short cook times; requires precise alignment and supervision.
materials: - Old satellite dish lined with mylar, foil tape, or mirror pieces
- Optional: large umbrella frame modified with reflective segments
- Sturdy stand or tripod to hold dish and align it with the sun
- Metal frame or cage at focal point to hold pot safely
- Black pressure cooker or frying pot (must handle high heat)
processSteps: 1. Line parabolic dish with reflective material, ensuring a clean, smooth curve.
2. Mark and test focal point using a piece of black paper (should burn in ~5 seconds under strong sun).
3. Mount pot holder securely at focal point using metal bars or cage.
4. Place black cooking pot with food or water inside the holder.
5. Align the parabola toward the sun and make periodic adjustments.
6. Supervise at all times — cook times may be as short as 10–30 minutes for boiling water or frying.
7. Remove food using heat-safe gloves and allow cooker to cool.

subcategories.title: Biogas
subcategories.description: A comprehensive guide to the materials required and the step-by-step process for planning, building, and operating a biogas digester.
subcategories.context: This module provides in-depth information on constructing and managing a biogas system. It covers necessary materials for various common digester types and outlines a multi-phase process from planning to safe operation and maintenance. The advice and cautions section (to be filled with your content) will complement this technical information.
materials: - Main digester vessel (e.g., 1000L-2000L IBC tote, multiple HDPE plastic drums, pre-fabricated tank, or materials for constructed digesters like bricks, cement, sand, and waterproofing agent for fixed-dome; or geomembrane for Puxin-type)
- Insulation materials (e.g., straw, styrofoam, agricultural plastic sheeting - especially for colder climates)
- PVC pipes (various diameters: e.g., 100-150mm for inlet, 50-100mm for outlet, 15-25mm for gas line)
- PVC fittings (elbows, T-joints, reducers, end caps, unions, tank connectors/bulkhead fittings)
- Ball valves or gate valves (for inlet, outlet, and gas line control)
- Sealants (e.g., PVC primer and cement, silicone sealant, rubber gaskets, Teflon tape) for watertight and airtight seals
- Gas holder/storage (e.g., inner tube of a truck tire, dedicated biogas storage bag with UV protection, or materials for a floating drum gasholder like a smaller drum and guide frame)
- Transparent flexible hose (for visual checks and connections)
- Condensate/Water trap (PVC components to build a U-trap or T-junction drain)
- H2S Scrubber (optional but recommended: PVC pipe section, end caps with fittings, iron filings/steel wool)
- Manometer (DIY U-tube with clear plastic tubing and colored water, or a low-pressure gauge)
- Pressure relief valve (set to a safe low pressure, e.g., 2-5 kPa)
- Flame arrestor (install on the gas line near the point of use)
- Buckets or containers for collecting and mixing feedstock
- Chopper, shredder, or machete (for reducing particle size of fibrous materials - optional)
- Basic hand tools (saw for PVC, drill, screwdrivers, wrenches, spirit level, measuring tape)
- Shovels, trowels (for excavation or concrete work if applicable)
- Biogas stove or burner (specifically designed for biogas or modified)
- Flexible gas piping for connecting to appliances
processSteps: - Step 1: Assess Feedstock Availability & Type (quantify daily organic waste like manure, kitchen scraps; analyze C/N ratio if possible)
- Step 2: Determine Energy Needs & System Sizing (calculate required gas volume, which dictates digester volume - typical retention times are 20-60 days)
- Step 3: Select Digester Design (e.g., floating drum, fixed dome, IBC tote, Puxin; consider climate, cost, available skills, and materials)
- Step 4: Detailed Site Selection (ensure level ground, sunlight (for some designs), proximity to feedstock and use-point, away from dwellings, consider effluent drainage)
- Step 5: Create a Detailed Construction Plan & Material List (sketch design, list all components, estimate costs)
- Step 6: Review Safety Regulations & Obtain Permits (if required locally)
- Step 7: Prepare the Site (clear vegetation, level ground, excavate if necessary for underground designs)
- Step 8: Construct or Place the Digester Tank (follow design plans meticulously; ensure structural integrity)
- Step 9: Install Inlet (for feeding) and Outlet (for digestate removal) Pipes (ensure correct height difference for gravity flow, airtight and watertight seals)
- Step 10: Assemble and Install Gas Holder/Dome and Gas Outlet Pipe (ensure gasholder can move freely if floating type, or dome is gas-tight)
- Step 11: Connect Gas Line with Valves, Manometer, H2S Scrubber, Water Trap, and Safety Devices (pressure relief valve, flame arrestor)

- Step 12: Perform Thorough Leak Testing (use soapy water on all gas joints and seals; for water seals, check levels. Pressurize slightly if possible to check tank integrity before filling with slurry)
- Step 13: Prepare Inoculum/Starter Culture (use slurry from an active digester, fresh cow dung, or septic tank sludge – about 10-30% of digester volume)
- Step 14: Prepare Initial Feedstock Slurry (mix organic waste with water to a suitable consistency, typically 1:1 to 1:4 solids to water ratio by weight, targeting 6-10% total solids)
- Step 15: Load the Digester (first add inoculum, then gradually fill with prepared feedstock slurry, leaving recommended headspace)
- Step 16: Seal the Digester and Monitor (allow 1-4 weeks for anaerobic conditions to establish and methane production to begin; initial gas will be mainly CO2 and should be vented safely)
- Step 17: Test First Biogas for Flammability (collect a sample in a small bag or balloon and test carefully away from the digester; if it burns with a blue flame, it's methane-rich)

- Step 18: Establish a Regular Feeding Schedule (daily or every few days, add a consistent amount of fresh slurry – e.g., 1/20th to 1/60th of the digester volume, matching the hydraulic retention time)
- Step 19: Simultaneous Digestate Removal (remove an equivalent volume of digestate as you feed to maintain liquid level)
- Step 20: Monitor Gas Production & Quality (check manometer, observe flame color when in use)
- Step 21: Utilize Biogas Safely (connect to appliances, ensure good ventilation where gas is used)
- Step 22: Process and Utilize Digestate (use as organic fertilizer after composting or dilution; handle with care)
- Step 23: Regular Checks (inspect for gas leaks, water seal levels, pipe blockages, structural integrity of the digester and gasholder)
- Step 24: Scum and Sludge Management (periodically check for and remove excessive scum buildup or sediment if design allows and performance degrades)
- Step 25: Maintain H2S Scrubber Material (replace iron filings/steel wool when saturated – color change or H2S smell indicates saturation)
- Step 26: Troubleshoot Common Issues (e.g., low/no gas, acidic conditions (low pH), foaming, rotten egg smell, refer to specific troubleshooting guides)
- Step 27: Follow Safety Protocols Continuously (no smoking, ensure flame arrestors are functional, handle digestate hygienically)

subcategories.title: DIY Biochar Retort (Soda Keg + Cast Iron Pan)
subcategories.description: A step-by-step guide for making biochar at home using a repurposed soda keg sealed with a cast iron pan and secured with stainless cable. The vessel is heated inside a wood stove to achieve pyrolysis.
subcategories.context: This module details the design, materials, and step-by-step process for building and operating a home-scale biochar retort using an improvised pressure vessel. It supports experimentation with different biomass types, carbon yields, and environmental impact (e.g., odor, residue, gas output). This system is well-suited for sustainable homesteads and regenerative agriculture enthusiasts.
materials: - Stainless steel soda keg (top removed to create a chamber)
- Cast iron pan (used as heavy lid)
- Stainless steel cable (7x woven over-under stitching to hold the lid down under thermal expansion)
- Optional: Furnace cement, clay, or fire rope gasket to improve the seal
- Dry wood chunks, nutshells, dried crop waste, or small sticks (low-moisture for optimal char quality)
- Wood stove or masonry heater with a well-established coal bed
- IR thermometer or thermocouple for vessel surface temp
- Ventilation (if indoors, use stove with chimney draw)
processSteps: - Step 1: Cut the soda keg and deburr edges
- Step 2: Select a cast iron pan that tightly fits the keg’s top
- Step 3: Prepare the stainless steel cable; test-fit the weave to hold the lid tight
- Step 4: Fill the keg with dry, uniform biomass (avoid green or wet material)
- Step 5: Place the lid and secure with cable (tighten using pliers or turnbuckle)
- Step 6: Optionally apply clay or ash at the seam
- Step 7: Prepare a bed of red-hot coals in the wood stove
- Step 8: Insert the sealed vessel into the coals
- Step 9: Let cook for 1.5–3 hours, depending on stove heat and biomass
- Step 10: Optionally add coals around the vessel for uniform heat
- Step 11: Allow the retort to cool fully (ideally overnight)
- Step 12: Open the vessel only when cold to avoid oxygen flash
- Step 13: Remove the biochar and inspect quality (black, glossy or dull, lightweight)
- Step 14: Store in airtight container or soak in compost tea before soil application
- Step 15: Optionally log temperature, biomass weight in/out, odor, texture for experiments

videos.title: Making Biochar at Home with a Simple Retort
videos.description: A demonstration of using a soda keg and cast iron pan to produce biochar.

notes: Do not open the vessel hot—risk of flash combustion!
This is a low-pressure system; never fully seal without a pressure vent.
Char yield will vary by biomass type, particle size, and cook time.
If syngas flames appear, they should be short-lived and low volume in this design.

Walls Made of Straw? Incredible Craftsmanship Before Cement
videos.description:
Jan 30, 2026  #TimberFrame #RuralLife #TraditionalConstruction
Before modern insulation materials, cement, and industrial construction methods became widespread, rural buildings relied on locally available resources.
In many parts of Germany, straw, clay, and wood were used to protect timber-framed houses from wind, rain, and cold — a practice that continued well into the 20th century, and in some regions even until the 1960s.

This film documents the traditional method of applying straw wall cladding to farmhouse buildings, using techniques once common in everyday rural life.
Step by step, the process shows how clay mortar, hazel rods, and long-stem rye straw were combined to create a durable, weather-resistant wall surface.

Through historical footage, Uncovered Past offers an authentic look at pre-industrial building knowledge, craftsmanship, and materials — preserved at a time when such methods were already disappearing.

brownfield.description: A property where redevelopment is complicated by real or suspected contamination. The EPA Brownfields program provides assessment and cleanup grants to return these sites to productive use.

subcategories.subtitle: Citizen-science protocols for tracking species and habitat health
subcategories.description: Practical field methods for documenting species presence and habitat condition at a site the community is invested in — the biodiversity-support counterpart to the decontamination work above, tracked through the same focus-area/project logging pipeline.

biodiversity.description: The variety of species and ecological communities present at a site — tracked over time as an indicator of habitat health, independent of any specific contamination question.

subcategories.title: Cyanobacteria & Harmful Algal Blooms
subcategories.subtitle: Identifying, reporting, and understanding HABs in lakes and ponds
subcategories.description: Harmful algal blooms (HABs) caused by cyanobacteria are appearing earlier, lasting longer, and occurring in waterbodies with no prior bloom history. Cyanobacteria produce cyanotoxins including microcystin (liver toxin), cylindrospermopsin (multi-organ toxin), and anatoxin-a (neurotoxin). This is the video-library companion to the 'Cyanobacteria Watch and Lake Health' program already documented for this platform.
subcategories.context: Matches Program 2 (Cyanobacteria Watch and Lake Health) in blog-east-coast-citizen-science-units.md — reporting goes to each state's HAB hotline (MA, NY, CT, VT, MD, VA, NJ all have active programs as of that writing).

videos.description: PLACEHOLDER — Target: how to deploy a Secchi disk, record transparency depth, and what a declining trend indicates about eutrophication risk.

cyanobacteria.description: Photosynthetic bacteria (not true algae) that can bloom under warm, calm, nutrient-rich conditions and produce cyanotoxins (microcystin, cylindrospermopsin, anatoxin-a). Blooms are becoming more frequent and widespread as waters warm.

subcategories.title: Climate-Driven Biological Exposure
subcategories.subtitle: Tick and mosquito range expansion, and other climate-linked health risks
subcategories.description: As winters shorten and warm, disease-vector ranges are expanding into areas with no prior exposure history — this subcategory is the video-library companion to the 'Tick Watch Northeast' program already documented for this platform, plus the broader pattern of climate-linked biological hazard shift.
subcategories.context: Matches Program 1 (Tick Watch Northeast) in blog-east-coast-citizen-science-units.md — habitat transect assessment and drag-cloth sampling protocols.

videos.description: PLACEHOLDER — Target: the standardised drag-cloth method (adapted from TickSpotters/URI protocol) for sampling tick density in a habitat transect, and how to record counts by life stage and species.

videos.title: Why Disease-Vector Ranges Are Shifting With a Warming Climate
videos.description: PLACEHOLDER — Target: a general-audience explainer connecting shorter/warmer winters to tick and mosquito range expansion into previously low-risk areas, without overstating any single event as proof of the trend.

tick-borne disease.description: Diseases (Lyme, anaplasmosis, babesiosis and others) transmitted by tick species whose range and active season are expanding as winters shorten — tracked here through habitat transect and drag-cloth sampling.

subcategories.title: Pollinator & Ecological Gardening
subcategories.subtitle: Designing gardens that support native pollinators and local ecological function
subcategories.description: Native-plant garden design for pollinator support and general ecological function — distinct from food production. Draws on the same native-species-over-invasive principle already established for rain garden planting in docs/eco-ops-workflow-guide.md, applied to pollinator habitat specifically.
subcategories.context: SPEC_ECOOPS_COMMUNITY_PLATFORM.md already names 'creating pollinator corridors in built environments' and community coordinator watch-lists for declining pollinators — this subcategory is the video-library companion to that.

Community watch-list of declining pollinator species

videos.title: Designing a Pollinator Garden With Native Plants
videos.description: PLACEHOLDER — Target: native plant selection for a pollinator garden, why regionally-native species outperform ornamental cultivars for pollinator support, and how to avoid inadvertently planting an invasive.

videos.description: PLACEHOLDER — Target: connecting fragmented pollinator habitat across a neighborhood or campus — verge plantings, linked garden beds, and how a corridor differs from an isolated garden.

pollinator corridor.description: A connected chain of pollinator-supporting habitat across a landscape, so pollinators can move between patches rather than being stranded in isolated gardens.

subcategories.title: Forest Gardening & Food Forestry
subcategories.subtitle: Seven-layer perennial food systems that mimic natural woodland
subcategories.description: Forest gardening (food forestry / permaculture agroforestry) cultivates perennial food-producing systems designed across seven layers — canopy, sub-canopy, shrub, herbaceous, groundcover, root zone, and vine. Once established, a forest garden produces food with dramatically less labour than annual vegetable gardening while providing wildlife habitat, carbon sequestration, and stormwater infiltration.
subcategories.context: Matches Part 3 (Forest Gardening) in docs/eco-ops-workflow-guide.md, including the seven-layer design and the 'eco:habitat — Community Forest Garden' certificate issued for a documented site.

videos.title: Designing a Seven-Layer Forest Garden
videos.description: PLACEHOLDER — Target: a walkthrough of the seven forest-garden layers (canopy through vine) and how they're planned together as one system rather than planted independently.

videos.title: Plant Guilds Explained — Companion Planting at Forest Scale
videos.description: PLACEHOLDER — Target: how a 'guild' (a small cluster of mutually-beneficial species, e.g. a fruit tree + nitrogen-fixer + groundcover) works, and how to design one for a specific site.

forest garden.description: A perennial food-producing system designed across seven vertical layers to mimic the structure of a natural woodland — lower labour than annual gardening once established, with habitat and stormwater benefits as a side effect.

subcategories.title: Expert-Coordinated Ecological Planning
subcategories.subtitle: Conservation biologists, coordinators, and community campaigns working from the same plan
subcategories.description: How a restoration or monitoring campaign actually gets designed and run at watershed or landscape scale: a conservation biologist or coordinator sets the plan and target species, community teams (schools, elders, volunteers) execute the fieldwork, and the resulting data flows back to refine the plan for the next season.
subcategories.context: Modelled directly on the watershed-campaign and lesson-endorsement examples in blog-costa-rica-biodiversity-platform.md — a SINAC-style coordinator running a multi-school stream-corridor campaign, and a conservation biologist's module being locally annotated by a practitioner before use.
materials: Campaign coordination record on the platform
processSteps: 1. Expert or coordinator designs the campaign and target species list
2. Local practitioner/elder reviews for real-world feasibility ('community annotation')
4. Data aggregates back to the coordinator/expert
5. Plan is revised for the next season

videos.title: How a Restoration Campaign Gets Designed and Run
videos.description: PLACEHOLDER — Target: a coordinator or conservation biologist walking through how a multi-site campaign (e.g. a stream-corridor restoration plan spanning several schools/communities) is designed, launched, and adjusted based on incoming field data.

videos.title: Riparian Buffer Planting — Species Selection for Flood Resilience
videos.description: PLACEHOLDER — Target: how a conservation biologist chooses native species and spacing for a riparian buffer, and the real tradeoff between fast-establishing exotics and slower-growing natives.

restoration planning.description: The expert-designed plan (target species, site selection, timeline) that a community campaign executes in the field — refined season over season as real field data comes back in.

subcategories.title: Elder Knowledge & Plant Nursery Networks
subcategories.subtitle: Pairing traditional ecological knowledge with the nurseries that can actually supply what a restoration plan needs
subcategories.description: An elder's diachronic knowledge of a site (which species pioneer naturally, which are hardest to establish, what the land looked like decades ago) is only actionable if paired with a real supply chain — a nursery network that knows which native species are actually obtainable versus theoretically correct but impossible to source. This subcategory pairs the elder-knowledge framework from docs/eco-ops-workflow-guide.md Part 7 with the nursery-sourcing role described for a Costa Rica pilot.
subcategories.context: A retired nursery worker who has propagated native species for decades qualifies for a Knowledge Keeper credential the same way a long-term site observer does — see the existing Knowledge Keeper reward path (src/data/rewards-catalog.ts, src/pages/KnowledgeKeepersPage.vue) and docs/eco-ops-workflow-guide.md Part 7's 'elder observation is primary data' principle.

2. Structured interview, with the elder controlling what stays public/community-only/private
3. Cross-reference recommended species against actual local nursery availability
5. Link the record to the relevant restoration campaign

videos.description: PLACEHOLDER — Target: a working native-plant nursery, what it actually takes to propagate a locally-appropriate species at scale, and how a restoration plan's 'ideal' species list gets corrected against what a nursery can really supply.

Knowledge Keeper.description: A community elder or long-term practitioner (site observer, nursery propagator, etc.) whose diachronic, place-specific knowledge is recognised with a platform credential — treated as primary data, not anecdote.

subcategories.title: Microplastics in Water Supply
subcategories.subtitle: Where they come from, and what treatment actually removes them
subcategories.description: Microplastics enter water supplies from textile-fiber shedding in laundry effluent, tire-wear road runoff, and the breakdown of larger plastic debris. They've been found in both bottled and tap water. Conventional (primary/secondary) wastewater treatment misses most microplastics — tertiary/membrane filtration is meaningfully more effective but not universally deployed.
subcategories.context: Membrane filtration (RO/NF) already appears in src/data/pfas-methods-library.ts as a PFAS method — it captures microplastics as a side effect of the same physical rejection mechanism, though that entry's citations are PFAS-specific and shouldn't be reused uncritically here.
materials: Lab-based particle analysis (field test kits cannot reliably quantify microplastics — no cheap validated method exists, the same honesty caveat as PFAS field testing)
processSteps: 1. Identify likely source pathways (laundry, stormwater, WWTP outfall)
3. Evaluate treatment stage (does the plant have tertiary filtration?)
4. Advocate for/install tertiary treatment where feasible

videos.title: Where Microplastics in Drinking Water Actually Come From
videos.description: PLACEHOLDER — Target: a clear explainer distinguishing textile-fiber, tire-wear, and plastic-fragment sources, and how each reaches a water supply differently.

videos.title: How Wastewater Treatment Plants Handle (and Miss) Microplastics
videos.description: PLACEHOLDER — Target: primary/secondary treatment's limited effectiveness versus tertiary/membrane filtration, ideally with a real plant walkthrough.

microplastics.description: Plastic particles smaller than 5mm, from fragmentation of larger debris or direct shedding (textile fibers, tire wear). Unlike PFAS, once dispersed into the environment they cannot practically be concentrated and removed at scale — source reduction is the primary lever.

subcategories.title: Microplastics in Food Supply
subcategories.subtitle: Seafood, salt, and agricultural soil
subcategories.description: Filter-feeding seafood (mussels, oysters) and some fish accumulate microplastics directly from water. Sea salt production has documented microplastic contamination. On land, plastic mulch film and biosolids/sewage-sludge fertilizer are documented pathways for microplastics entering agricultural soil and, from there, crops.
subcategories.context: Biosolids as fertilizer is a genuine tradeoff — it recycles nutrients but is also a documented microplastic (and, separately, PFAS) pathway into soil. Treat 'biosolids are contaminated' and 'biosolids have real agronomic value' as both true rather than picking one.
processSteps: 1. Identify the pathway of concern (seafood, salt, or soil)
2. Lab-based sampling where a claim will be made publicly
3. For soil: check plastic mulch and biosolids sourcing practices
4. Log findings to the platform record

videos.title: Microplastics in Seafood and Sea Salt — What's Actually Been Found
videos.description: PLACEHOLDER — Target: a survey of real published findings on microplastics in shellfish, fish, and sea salt, honest about how much variation exists between studies and locations.

videos.title: Plastic Mulch and Biosolids — How Microplastics Get Into Farm Soil
videos.description: PLACEHOLDER — Target: how plastic mulch film fragments in place and how biosolids fertilizer carries microplastics into soil, presented alongside the real agronomic value biosolids also provide.

biosolids.description: Treated sewage sludge applied to agricultural land as fertilizer — recycles nutrients but is a documented pathway for both microplastics and PFAS into soil. Genuinely a tradeoff, not a simple good/bad.

subcategories.title: Microplastics & Human Health — What's Actually Known
subcategories.subtitle: Detected in the body; health effects are still being studied
subcategories.description: Microplastics have been detected in human blood, lung tissue, and placenta — that part is documented. What those findings mean for actual health outcomes is still an active, unsettled research area. Treat any claim of a specific disease or health effect with the same skepticism this library already applies to PFAS phytoremediation claims: state what's detected plainly, and don't imply a causal health claim the current evidence doesn't support.
subcategories.context: This is the microplastics equivalent of the phytoremediation entry in src/data/pfas-methods-library.ts — real detection, unsettled causal science. Any video chosen here should be reviewed for whether it overstates certainty before it's approved.

videos.title: Microplastics Detected in the Human Body — What We Actually Know (and Don't)
videos.description: PLACEHOLDER — Target: an honest explainer distinguishing 'detected in tissue X' (established) from 'causes health effect Y' (not established) — prefer a source that makes this distinction explicitly rather than one that blurs it for effect.

videos.title: How People Are Exposed — Ingestion, Inhalation, and Dermal Routes
videos.description: PLACEHOLDER — Target: the three exposure routes (eating/drinking, breathing airborne fibers/dust, skin contact) without overstating relative risk between them, since that's still being studied.

emerging research.description: Detection of microplastics in human tissue is documented; causal health-effect research is still active and unsettled, the same maturity distinction this library already draws for PFAS phytoremediation.

subcategories.title: Reducing Microplastic Pollution at the Source
subcategories.subtitle: Once dispersed, they can't practically be cleaned up — source reduction is the real lever
subcategories.description: Unlike PFAS or heavy metals, dispersed microplastic particles cannot be concentrated and removed from soil or ocean sediment at any meaningful scale. That makes source reduction — not cleanup — the primary practical intervention: washing-machine fiber filters, tire-wear particle capture, reduced single-use plastic that fragments into secondary microplastics, and (already largely achieved in many jurisdictions) microbead bans in personal care products.
subcategories.context: This is the honest limitations section for the whole Microplastics area — pair it with the Water Supply subcategory's treatment content so the two together don't imply cleanup is a solved problem.
materials: Washing-machine microfiber filter (e.g. external filter bag/unit)
processSteps: 1. Identify the highest-impact source for your context (textile, tire, packaging)
2. Install or advocate for source-capture technology

videos.title: Washing Machine Filters — Capturing Textile Microfibers Before They Reach Waterways
videos.description: PLACEHOLDER — Target: how an external or built-in washing-machine microfiber filter works and how much fiber shedding it actually captures.

videos.title: Tire Wear Particles — The Overlooked Microplastic Source
videos.description: PLACEHOLDER — Target: how tire wear generates microplastic particles at a scale that rivals or exceeds other sources, and what municipal-scale capture (e.g. roadside drain filters) looks like.

source reduction.description: Preventing microplastics from entering the environment in the first place — the only practical lever available, since dispersed particles cannot be cleaned up at scale once released.
